items.title: Kimi continues to challenge the frontier with K3.1 Pro
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 10,866 new readers. The frontier leaders keep warning that China’s open models are closing in. For the past year, Moonshot’s Kimi has been the fastest one on the frontier’s tail.

The company’s new K3.1 Pro now trails only Anthropic’s and Meta’s top models in independent rankings, and the free weights coming soon would make it the strongest open model yet. Scores like these are usually the bat signal for Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s next industry-moving releases.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Kimi continues to challenge the frontier with K3.1 Pro

  • The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

  • Let AI sign in without sharing your passwords

  • Canva’s first in-house image model climbs the ranks

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

MOONSHOT AI

🌙 Kimi continues to challenge the frontier with K3.1 Pro

Image source: Moonshot

The Rundown: Chinese AI lab Moonshot just introduced Kimi K3.1 Pro, an upgrade to its July K3 model that it says is “matching the strongest proprietary models” on key benchmarks, with free-to-download weights set to come by Nov. 4.

The details:

  • Artificial Analysis placed it No. 4 overall on its Intelligence Index, beating OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and trailing only Anthropic’s 5.5 duo and Meta’s Muse Wonder.

  • In Moonshot’s tests, K3.1 Pro tops Opus 5.5 on hours-long coding projects, expert academic questions, document-heavy research, and real-world job tasks.

  • At $2 in/$10 out per million tokens, K3.1 Pro is priced like Sonnet 5.5, a fifth of Astra’s rate, but consumes tokens at a higher rate than its frontier rivals.

  • AA also ranks it the best openly available cyber-defense model, scoring 64% with no safety refusals, trailing just a GPT-6 variant available only to vetted defenders.

Why it matters: U.S. labs have kept their best hacking models locked down, but a Chinese model now sits just behind OAI’s gated cyber model. Dario Amodei gave defenders 6-12 months in May before Chinese models catch up, and K3.1 Pro is already near the top on defense — with open models’ attack skills also likely not far behind.

TOGETHER WITH GARTNER

💭 Rethink your enterprise app strategy    

The Rundown: Megavendors still control enterprise software today, but for how long? With AI reshaping how apps are built and licensed, this Gartner webinar shows how to use SaaS renewals for flexibility, cut hidden API costs, and govern AI outcomes.

In this webinar, you'll learn how to:

  • Escape vendor lock-in at renewal

  • Avoid hidden API costs

  • Prepare to govern AI outcomes

Register today.

THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE

💡 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.

Jonah, Head of AI Education: My wife and I used ChatGPT to bring our vision for a new master bedroom to life instead of hiring a designer.

We started by sketching the basic layout, which ChatGPT rendered into a floor plan. We identified the wood, the type of cut we wanted, and the finishes. Then we had a detailed conversation about what we wanted the room to look like from each side.

For smaller details, we scanned Google Images and Pinterest for inspiration pictures and designs we liked. We used ChatGPT Voice for back-and-forth conversations and final tweaks, re-rendering the images as our ideas developed.

We took the final images to our contractor to help him understand the higher-level vision we wanted to achieve.

Jennifer, Tech & Robotics Writer: We’re narrowing down high school options for my daughter, who wants to focus on art. I’m using Astra to find public schools in our area and beyond with strong art programs and understand how they compare.

Astra can research school rankings and academic results, review art courses and facilities, and bring admissions requirements, portfolio expectations, fees, and commute times into one clear comparison. It can also suggest preparation classes—such as drawing, painting, digital art, or portfolio workshops—based on what each school expects.

From there, it’s helping me build a shortlist, organize open days and application deadlines, and prepare questions for school visits. We can work through the options together and find a school she’s excited about.

AI TRAINING

🔐 Let AI sign in without sharing your passwords

The Rundown: In this guide, you will use 1Password to approve an AI assistant’s login without pasting a password into chat. You’ll deny one request, test a small reading task, and check that access ends when you’re done.

Step-by-step:

  1. Check whether your agent has the official 1Password connection. Muse and Grok Bot are rolling it out, while Claude has a separate Mac setup

  2. Choose a test account with no private data or saved payment details. Save its login in 1Password and sign out in the browser the agent will use

  3. Give the agent a page to read and rule out edits, messages, and purchases. Check the site and saved login in the 1Password request, then deny the request

  4. Start again and approve the correct test login. Check that the agent reads the right page without changing anything or asking for a password in chat

  5. Stop the task, sign out of the website, and remove the 1Password connection. Check the browser as well as the connection settings

Pro tip: Removing a password connection may leave a website signed in. Check both before you finish.

PRESENTED BY OPENART

🎨 Create ad variations to scale performance marketing

The Rundown: Have an ad that’s performing well? Or an ad format that inspires you? OpenArt’s Ad Remake makes it easy to create your own versions with your product, branding, and style — giving you more ads to test without starting from scratch.

OpenArt Ad Remake lets you:

  • Keep the hook, pacing, and structure that work

  • Swap in your product, characters, and language without reshooting

  • Adapt ads to 9:16, 16:9, 1:1, and 4:5 formats

Try Ad Remake.

CANVA

🎨 Canva’s first in-house image model climbs the ranks

Image source: Canva

The Rundown: Canva just launched Craft, the company’s first in-house AI image model, debuting at No. 4 on DesignArena’s crowdsourced leaderboard behind only three OpenAI models.

The details:

  • Craft was trained on millions of designer-made templates like menus, slides, and posters from the company’s own library.

  • The model plans each layout before drawing it with a two-step architecture, so images convert easily into editable designs via a Magic Layers feature.

  • Craft’s 1340 score on the DesignArena beats the top models from Microsoft, Google, and xAI, while also landing No. 1 overall in portrait and nature categories.

  • Craft is live for all Canva platform users and via public API, with MCP access for external assistants and agents also on the way.

Why it matters: Canva has an endless supply of training data, and Craft’s strong results show how powerful that can be for building an in-house model. While legacy competitors have been reeling amid the AI boom, Canva’s integrations and now its own AI model put near frontier-level image capabilities in front of 250M+ users on its own terms.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Bridget built a gym log that updates itself every Friday

Today’s workflow comes from reader Bridget Overson:

“Every Friday at 10 a.m. ET, a scheduled Claude agent refreshes a living 'Hevy Workout Log' document with that week's strength-training data, body measurements, and a progress photo. The automation runs fully unattended, with no human in the loop after the owner sets it up.

The agent pulls information from three independent systems: the Hevy fitness-tracking API, a Google Drive photo folder, and the living document. It reconciles those sources against a date range, determines what's new versus already recorded, and writes structured, formatted updates in the correct places. This requires more judgment than a simple script or webhook.

Claude Docs, through a Claude Artifact, is the living document: it has one tab for each weekday and a Weekly Summary tab. There is no custom backend, database, or glue code. Because the workflow runs on a schedule without anyone watching, its specification requires a notification every time, including when nothing changed.”

items.title: SAP's Philipp Herzig on AI built for business data
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}. AI coding tools can spin up an app in minutes, and plenty of people have taken that as a sign traditional software is finished. SAP’s CTO thinks they’re missing the harder part: running a business on that app.

In partnership with SAP, we sat down with CTO Philipp Herzig to talk about the “SaaS is dead” debate, how AI is changing the way people use work software, what agents need to know to get answers right, how to keep AI bills in check, and the models built for business data.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • What the “SaaS is dead” narrative misses

  • From clicking screens to stating intent

  • Teaching AI how your business runs

  • Cheaper tokens, better business outcomes

  • Specialized AI for decisions that count

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

INDUSTRY TAKE

🏢 What the “SaaS is dead” narrative misses

Image credits: Kiki Wu / The Rundown

The Rundown: As AI coding tools let anyone build apps, many believe traditional software companies are over. Herzig thinks this narrative confuses building an app with running one, and says the same gap explains why so many AI pilots never make it to production.

Cheung: What’s one AI trend you think is overhyped?

Herzig: The idea that “SaaS is dead” because AI can now write software. It confuses the ability to generate an application with the responsibility of running it.

Generating an expense app is one thing. Running it across 40 countries, keeping up with tax rules, enforcing permissions, and reconciling reimbursements is another. As agents take on more autonomous work, they depend more on trusted data, business context, governance, and security. The interface can change radically. The need for reliable business processes doesn’t.

Cheung: Why do so many AI pilots never get deployed?

Herzig: The difference between a prototype and a production-ready system at enterprise scale, with all the technological dependencies and complexity under the hood while still looking simple for the user, is still substantial human work.

Cheung: What’s been harder at SAP, the technology or adoption?

Herzig: Adoption, without a doubt. Useful AI changes who makes which decisions and how. That affects expertise, authority, and professional identity.

The companies moving fastest gave access to people whose judgment the organization already trusted. A respected supply chain manager saying “this helped me catch a disruption” is more powerful than any training program.

Why it matters: SAP has an obvious stake in defending enterprise software, but the gap between generating an app and running a business on it is real. If you’re rolling out AI at work, his adoption advice applies regardless of vendor: pick one high-value use case and put the colleagues people already trust first in line.

AI IRL

💻 From clicking screens to stating intent

Image credits: Kiki Wu / The Rundown

The Rundown: SAP’s newest AI push, Joule Work, flips how people use business software: instead of clicking through screens, you say what you want done. Herzig walked us through how it works, how he uses it himself, and what it means for developers.

Cheung: How does Joule Work change the day-to-day experience of using business software?

Herzig: For decades, enterprise software required us to learn its structure: which application to open, which screen to find, which buttons to click. With Joule Work, you start with what you want to accomplish. It brings together information and capabilities across applications.

But this isn’t about replacing every screen with a chat box. With Spaces, Joule can turn your intent into a personalized visual workspace: a chart, table, or dashboard you refine by asking. I don’t have to log into four systems, orient myself, and hope I’m looking at the right data. The relevant picture is already assembled. Web, desktop, mobile, and voice let you work in the way that fits the moment.

Cheung: What’s one way you use it yourself?

Herzig: As CTO, I want to stay close to what our engineers are building. But the question for me isn’t just “What changed?” It’s “Where would my attention be useful?” Instead of piecing together an update, I can ask Joule to bring the relevant changes together. That helps me arrive at a team conversation better informed: what should we discuss, what needs a closer look, and where can I help?

Joule doesn’t make those judgments for me. It reduces the work of gathering the information behind them. I spend less time collecting status and more time having conversations that move the work forward.

Cheung: If anyone can build with AI, what’s left for developers to do?

Herzig: The job shifts from implementation to architecture and judgment: deciding what’s worth building, evaluating business correctness, designing the system that governs agents safely, and handling edge cases and failures. The hardest engineering challenges in enterprise AI aren’t about building something that works. They’re about building something that works safely, at scale, with the right guardrails in place.

Joule Studio (SAP’s tool for building custom AI agents) removes that baseline burden. Developers start with the enterprise context, such as authentication, permissions, and compliance, already in place and focus on what delivers value.

Why it matters: If your company is handing employees agents and AI coding tools, Herzig’s point is that the easy part got easier and the hard part didn’t. Someone still has to own whether the output is correct, secure, and safe to act on, and that job is landing on developers.

EDUCATING AI

🧠 Teaching AI how your business runs

Image credits: Kiki Wu / The Rundown

The Rundown: Herzig says the riskiest AI answers are “fluent-but-wrong”: confident, correctly worded, and blind to how the business runs. SAP’s fix is giving agents a map of what company data means, plus a record of how past decisions got made.

Cheung: Most people might think giving AI access to their company’s files is enough context. What does AI actually need to know about a business to get answers right?

Herzig: Enterprise data lives in tables, and knowing what a field means requires understanding the business process behind it: the transactions, the unwritten rules and exceptions, and identity, like knowing a supplier in procurement is the same entity in finance.

The main risk in enterprise AI is fluent-but-wrong: an answer that sounds authoritative but is contextually off.

Cheung: SAP’s Knowledge Graph maps what a company’s data means. How does that make AI better in a business context?

Herzig: It gives models a machine-readable map of business objects, relationships, and rules. Agents stop guessing what fields mean.

That improves accuracy, reduces incorrect API calls and retries, and can give smaller models enough context for more tasks. But understanding a rule isn’t the same as enforcing it: actions still run with the user’s permissions, defined boundaries, and human approval where required.

Cheung: SAP is also building Company Memory to capture how work actually gets done. What’s the most useful thing it stores?

Herzig: The most valuable thing it stores is why an exception was approved: the context, rationale, authority, and outcome. The next person doesn’t have to start from scratch.

An exception must not become a rule just because it worked once. A human process owner must review it to understand why the decision worked, whether the conditions still apply, and whether it is safe to generalize.

Why it matters: If your team is wiring agents into real workflows, more documents in the prompt won’t fix fluent-but-wrong answers. An easy check: feed the agent inputs your real system would reject, like an invoice with no currency, and see what it accepts.

TOKENOMICS

💸 Cheaper tokens, better business outcomes

Image credits: Kiki Wu / The Rundown

The Rundown: Token prices keep falling, but company AI bills keep rising as usage spreads. Herzig says the question is shifting from who has the smartest model to who gets the best business result for the lowest cost.

Cheung: What did SAP learn as employee AI use grew?

Herzig: We cannot blindly throw everything at LLMs. An email summary doesn’t need the same model as complex, multi-step business reasoning. Route tasks by complexity, risk, and context, or solve them without an LLM call.

Reduce unnecessary token consumption without losing relevant context, including running models locally where it makes sense, so that only what actually requires LLM reasoning reaches the model. Keep models replaceable as quality and costs improve. And test at production scale: more than 60,000 SAP colleagues use Joule Work internally.

Cheung: Where do companies waste the most money on AI?

Herzig: Sending everything to frontier models, and “context bloat”: excessive, low-value information. A cheap model that is unreliable at scale isn’t a good trade either. The goal is the best outcome at the lowest possible cost.

Cheung: McKinsey found 80% of AI users feel more productive, but only 6% of companies see significant profit impact. What else closes that gap?

Herzig: In knowledge-intensive industries, people are the primary cost, so faster research, drafting, and coding can translate into margin. In capital-intensive businesses, assets, energy, and logistics can matter far more than payroll. Here, better demand forecasts or maintenance decisions may have a larger impact than faster writing. That’s why we invest in tabular AI. It’s ideal for predicting values in structured business data.

Why it matters: If your company’s AI costs are climbing, start with Herzig’s two culprits: top-tier models doing work a smaller one could handle, and prompts stuffed with information the model doesn’t need. And if your business runs on assets more than people, the bigger payoff may come from better forecasts, not faster writing.

TABULAR AI

📊 Specialized AI for decisions that count

Image credits: Kiki Wu / The Rundown

The Rundown: Tabular AI brings the foundation-model approach to spreadsheets and databases, and the space is heating up. SAP built its own SAP-RPT models, acquired Prior Labs, and committed more than €1B to it over four years, while Google and NVIDIA have also released tabular models of their own.

Cheung: For a company that’s never used a tabular model, what’s a good first problem to try?

Herzig: Start with use cases like payment delay prediction or cash flow forecasting. For payment delays, you need historical invoice dates, due dates, actual payment dates, customers, amounts, and a few contextual attributes.

With a few thousand rows, a Tabular Foundation Model can begin predicting when a customer will pay and flag likely delays while you still have options. Reducing average collection time from 50 to 45 days at a large company can free up tens of millions in cash.

Cheung: How can people judge whether to trust a prediction?

Herzig: SAP-RPT-1.6 offers Explain by Feature, showing which variables influenced a prediction, and Explain by Example, showing similar historical records used as evidence. A finance controller can assess whether those patterns still apply.

The longer-term ambition is causal reasoning: not just predicting a late payment, but understanding which intervention, such as a change of payment terms, would change it. That’s a research direction beyond explaining a prediction.

Why it matters: If most of your company’s AI use is chat and writing help, this is a low-cost way to test something different. The late-payment data already sits in most finance systems, the payoff is easy to measure, and the explanations let your finance team check the model’s work.

GO DEEPER

🎟️ Join the SAP TechEd experience

Herzig is scheduled to deliver the SAP TechEd keynote on Oct. 27, kicking off three days of virtual sessions on building AI-powered systems that move from intent to execution.

Register for the virtual event.

See you soon,

Rowan, Zach, Shubham, Jennifer, and Nate — the humans behind The Rundown

items.title: U.S. banks catch AI agents going off-script
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 6,202 new readers. AI agents have been pitched as the ultimate time-saver, handling digital chores so you don’t have to. Now those same capabilities are causing headaches for America’s banking ecosystem.

Some of the top banks in the country are spotting AI agents logging into customer accounts and taking actions… And they are having a hard time telling whether it’s a user-approved agent or one going rogue.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Banks crack down on AI agents’ account access

  • Rowan’s Corner: Safeguard yourself from AI hacks

  • Put your open Chrome tabs to work

  • Microsoft’s AI out-diagnoses doctors on hard cases

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

AI AGENTS

🏦 Banks crack down on AI agents’ account access

Image source: Images 2.5 / The Rundown

The Rundown: Top U.S. banks, including JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Morgan Stanley, are restricting third-party AI agents after finding them operating inside customer accounts, with some acting beyond instructions, Axios reported.

The details:

  • The banks caught agents logging in with customers’ own credentials, against their rules, with some calling support lines or taking actions users never requested.

  • Executives called the situation “horrifying,” fearing agents might hallucinate and hit users’ finances if they’re granted authority to make purchases or move funds.

  • While most cases involved user-authorized agents, not a rogue hack, one bank executive did tell Axios that they’re struggling to tell the two apart.

  • In response, Morgan Stanley is blocking third-party agents, and JPMorgan, BofA, and Citi are restricting them, with most banks moving toward read-only access.

Why it matters: Most of the worry here comes from AI misreading instructions and acting beyond requirements, with real money at stake. With agent use growing, blanket blocks can’t last forever, but they do buy banks enough time to build frameworks that let cleared agents take defined actions and catch rogue ones (which are also growing).

TOGETHER WITH GARTNER

🔮 7 AI themes shaping the future

The Rundown: From strategy and operations to talent, technology, investment, and governance, understanding these seven AI themes helps leaders align across functions to make smarter decisions.

In this webinar, you’ll learn:

  • 7 AI themes Gartner believes will have the greatest impact over the next 12 months

  • How these themes shape risk, opportunities, and priorities

  • Key actions to respond to these shifts

Watch now.

ROWAN’S CORNER

🔒 Safeguard yourself from AI hacks

Rowan: If you’re reading this newsletter, you’re probably the most AI-literate person your family knows. That comes with a responsibility that’s worth talking about this week.

Over the past few days, we’ve seen a massive spike in malicious AI attacks, and it’s likely going to get worse (and weirder) as the internet figures out how to secure things properly. Instead of panicking, take extra precautions now.

Here’s my protection list (forward it to your family, too):

  1. Set a family code word that any caller must say before you believe an emergency, and share it in person, never over text.

  2. Hang up and call back on the number you already have saved for any urgent money request, because AI can now clone anyone’s voice from seconds of audio.

  3. Set up 2FA on your logins, preferably with an authenticator app rather than SMS.

  4. Use a good password manager (like 1Password) with zero duplicated passwords, so one leaked login can’t unlock your whole life.

  5. Update everything today (browsers, phones, laptops, desktop apps), since this week’s certificate compromise made unpatched software the open door.

  6. Confirm any payment request on a second channel, different from the one it arrived on.

If you’re a builder, I also recommend using OpenAI’s free checker to see whether your website’s PHP version is exposed to the latest vulnerability.

AI TRAINING

🌐 Put your open Chrome tabs to work

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use ChatGPT’s updated Chrome extension to compare open pages, check the facts, and group the tabs you need. Start in Chat to read, then use Work for a browser action you approve.

Step-by-step:

  1. Install the official ChatGPT extension from OpenAI and open its side panel. Use a practice Chrome profile with public pages for your first run

  2. Open three pricing pages and tell ChatGPT which tabs to read. Give it your team size, required features, budget, and billing period

  3. Check the comparison against the pages. Confirm the full team cost and leave missing details unverified rather than guessing

  4. Switch to Work where available and ask it to group only those three tabs. Review the list first, then check the actual group in Chrome

  5. Ask for a short recommendation with source links and one question to resolve. Keep trials, purchases, and messages outside the task

Pro tip: A monthly price paid once a year is not a month-to-month offer. Check the billing label before comparing totals. Pro members get the comparison brief, prompt cards, and review checklist.

PRESENTED BY GRANOLA

🗓️ Your meetings, slides included

The Rundown: Granola is the AI notepad for people with back-to-back meetings. With Snapshots, you can save what’s shared on screen in a call to your notes. Later, ask about the meeting and the slide comes up with the answer.

Granola now lets you:

  • Save slides, dashboards, and docs from calls

  • Keep slides with your meeting notes

  • Find the slide when you need it

Get your first month on us with code THERUNDOWN.

AI RESEARCH

🩺 Microsoft’s AI out-diagnoses doctors on hard cases

Image source: Microsoft AI

The Rundown: Microsoft just published initial results from its MAI-DxO AI diagnostic system, revealing that it beats physicians on both complex medical cases and everyday ER visits while ordering fewer, cheaper tests at the same time.

The details:

  • MAI-DxO works like a virtual panel of doctors, with AI agents proposing diagnoses, ordering tests, and challenging each other as new results come in.

  • On 304 complex ‘New England Journal of Medicine’ cases, it more than doubled physicians’ accuracy with reference tools; on typical ER cases, it hit 80% vs. 47%.

  • One setup reached 81% accuracy on the NEJM cases at less than half the cost of comparable systems, with the gains holding even with newer models like GPT-5.5.

  • Microsoft will test the system in real clinical settings at Beth Israel Deaconess in Boston, measuring how its patient diagnoses fare against clinicians’ assessments.

Why it matters: Microsoft’s ER findings make a strong case for AI in diagnosis, but getting the assessment right is only one step in care. For AI to truly help patients, it will also need to guide treatment, track health over time, and fit into how doctors and patients make decisions together, all of which still have to be proven at scale.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Ben built a live task dashboard with a Raspberry Pi and Claude

Today’s workflow comes from reader Ben Blay:

I built a module that runs in MagicMirror on a Raspberry Pi and displays a real-time to-do list on a television in my office.

Claude does an admirable job managing my daily task list, which is stored in TASKS.md on my local computer. I wanted an at-a-glance dashboard showing everything I have in progress, sorted by priority and synchronized with that file.

I described the goal to Claude Code. Since I already had an old Raspberry Pi 3 and an off-the-shelf widescreen TV in my office, Claude Code suggested running MagicMirror on the Pi and Syncthing on both the Pi and my local computer to keep the file updated.

Claude then built the MagicMirror module to read TASKS.md. After a few tweaks to remove the default modules and clean up the spacing between items, the display was up and running. I set MagicMirror to start automatically when the Pi boots, so now my to-do list is in front of me all day.

See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub →

items.title: AI finds a security hole in 70% of the web
items.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 15,837 new readers. Just months ago, GPT-5.6 Sol made headlines for hacking Hugging Face. Now, the same model is on the other side of the fence, catching “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

OpenAI’s last-gen model helped researchers identify two critical flaws in PHP, the code behind about 70% of the web, sending IT teams worldwide into scramble mode — and the company says it has more major security finds like this still waiting to be disclosed.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • OpenAI’s model helps catch critical PHP flaws

  • Nate’s Notebook: If it’s copy-paste, let AI do it

  • Let Town prepare your next meeting brief

  • Anthropic joins the personal agent game with Duet

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

OPENAI

🚨 OpenAI’s model helps catch critical PHP flaws

Image source: X / The Rundown

The Rundown: PHP, the coding language behind ~70% of websites, just pushed patches for two critical flaws caught with OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, with the National Security Agency urging anyone who can’t patch right away to pull systems offline.

The details:

  • Security firm Calif found the first bug on Aug. 1 using 5.6 Sol, and Google-owned Wiz separately caught both weeks later with Sol and Gemini 4 Argon.

  • OpenAI said it worked on patches alongside the PHP maintainers for two months, calling the find “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

  • The decade-old bugs let hackers hijack servers with no login, and OpenAI calls them two of “several significant vulnerabilities” it’s still fixing.

  • Governments in Finland, Germany, and the Netherlands pulled websites offline, with Cloudflare saying it was “seeing early attacks emerging.”

Why it matters: PHP is used on 70% of websites, making the scale of this vulnerability massive — and yet it wasn’t turned into a working attack until a model now far behind the frontier was pointed at it. Pre-AI code is far more fragile than anyone imagined, and the only hope is that the good guys (and AI) can stay a step ahead of the exploits.

TOGETHER WITH GOOGLE FOR STARTUPS

💼 Gemini 4 Argon founder briefing

The Rundown: Google Cloud invites startup founders to an exclusive briefing with the Google DeepMind team to break down the newly announced Gemini 4 Argon model, exploring game-changing use cases and technical enhancements.

In this session, you’ll get:

  • A technical recap of Argon’s latest capabilities

  • DeepMind's perspective on high-impact startup use cases

  • Direct, unfiltered Q&A with the DeepMind team

Register for the briefing.

NATE’S NOTEBOOK

🔌 Nate’s Notebook: If it’s copy-paste, let AI do it

The Rundown: Each week, Rundown AI educator Nate Grahek breaks down what he’s seeing while teaching real teams to use AI.

Nate: If AI still isn’t making you faster, look at where your time goes. You’re searching for the right email, attaching the doc, compiling the context it needs. Then, once the work’s done, you’re copying and pasting everything it made back into the places it belongs.

My rule: if it’s as simple as a copy and paste, AI should be doing it for you through a connector.

Connectors also clear the nice-to-do pile. Everyone has a survey they’ve been meaning to send. It’s the kind of finishing touch that takes good work to great, and the first thing to go when we’re squished.

Hook your AI up to Tally or Jotform, and the whole loop happens without leaving chat: brainstorm the questions, build the form, draft the email to your audience, then pull the responses back in and make sense of them. Not a survey person? Find the finishing touch that lives in one or two tools you could connect today.

I sat on the sidelines over security, too. Now my ladder is read, then write, then send. Surveys are a safe first rung; nothing goes out by accident. Draft and critique everything in chat first. When it touches your inbox, it writes the draft, and you hit send.

Online banking felt risky too, until one day you stopped going to the branch. By next fall, most of us won’t open our inbox first. Our agent will have already triaged it and pitched us a short list of projects to say yes or no to.

Which app would you let your AI read first: inbox, drive, or calendar?

AI TRAINING

🗓️ Let Town prepare your next meeting brief

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll use Town, a business-focused personal AI assistant, to turn email and calendar details into a meeting brief. You’ll catch an unconfirmed time change, check the open work, and save the process for reuse.

Step-by-step:

  1. Sign up for Town and connect an approved Google test account. Keep changes behind approval and review any routines already running

  2. Add the guide’s fictional emails and private calendar event. Ask your Townie to read those exact sources and prepare a short brief in the conversation

  3. Check the meeting time, launch date, budget, and open tasks. A request to move a meeting should stay separate from the time still on the calendar

  4. Update the test event and send the confirming email. Ask for a fresh brief and check that only the changed facts move with it

  5. Save the process as a routine that runs only when you choose. Inspect its tools, delivery, and first result before adding a daily schedule

Pro tip: Town’s read-only routines can still email reports to you. Check the recipient and delivery settings as well as the mode. Pro members get the practice emails, prompts, and answer key.

PRESENTED BY VANTA

🍀 Spoiler: it wasn’t luck

The Rundown: Competition’s tough for startups, and everyone needs an edge. Nothing kills a deal faster than showing up without a SOC 2, but audit prep takes time most teams don’t have. Vanta gets you SOC 2-ready fast.

See for yourself:

  • 20% shorter enterprise deal cycles

  • $1.5M in sales unlocked in 3 months

  • SOC 2 Type II readiness in 3 weeks

Request a demo.

ANTHROPIC

🤖 Anthropic joins the personal agent game with Duet

Image source: Anthropic / The Rundown

The Rundown: Anthropic just introduced Claude Duet, an Opus 5.5-powered personal agent standalone app that can take proactive actions, work 24/7 (even when closed), and carry out tasks on its own cloud computer.

The details:

  • Example tasks include morning briefs, tracking calendars, and booking meetings, with Duet able to use its own computer even when devices are off.

  • Duet carries over memory, skills, and connectors from the Claude app, and also gains payment functionality via a one-time virtual card from Stripe’s Link wallet.

  • Anthropic put a focus on security and safety for Duet, with any deletion, payment, signature, or outgoing message needing user sign-off first.

  • Duet conversations count as part of normal Claude usage limits, with the research preview rolling out in waves to waitlisted U.S. Max and Pro subscribers.

Why it matters: The personal agent trend is already overflowing, and we’d agree… With this one exception. Anthropic’s models are in a class of their own right now, and while Grok Bot already borrows Claude for some tasks, Duet is the only one built entirely around Opus 5.5 — a model so good it could be the edge that separates it from the pack.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ Shimon built an AI donor tracker that flags who hasn’t given yet

Today’s workflow comes from reader Shimon:

“I built an AI fundraising campaign assistant with Make.com. The workflow reads emails sent from the crowdfunding platform used for the campaign, extracts the relevant information, and records it in a spreadsheet.

It also uses spreadsheets from previous years’ campaigns to maintain a list of people who have not donated to this campaign yet but have donated in the past. I can ask the agent questions by email, such as who has already donated. It can also answer questions with specific parameters, such as who has not donated but previously gave more than $1,000, or how much a specific person donated.

I built the workflow in Make using its AI tools. I connected it to a Gmail account, a Google Drive account containing the spreadsheets, and a ChatGPT account that processes the information as the AI agent.”

See the workflow on our Community Workflow Hub →
